Present ambiguous stimuli such as inkblots (Rorschach) or pictures (TAT) with the assumption that test takers will project their unconscious thoughts or feelings onto the stimuli (according to psychoanalytic approach).
Positive, helpful, and constructive behavior.
Our memory to perform a planned action or remembering to perform that planned action.
A mental image or “best example” that incorporates all the features you associate with a particular category.
Medical doctor and mental health professional who can prescribe medication or perform surgery.
A chemical that can pass through the blood-brain barrier to alter perception, thinking, behavior, and mood.
Freudian form of therapy involving free association, dream analysis, resistance, and transference aimed at providing the patient insight into his or her unconscious motivations and conflicts.
A therapist who has taken specialized training in psychoanalysis generally after earning either an MD or a PhD.
Psychological perspective concerned with how unconscious instincts, conflicts, motives, and defenses influence behavior.
Intense desire to achieve a drugged state in spite of adverse effects.
The science of behavior and mental processes.
Focus on methods for acquiring and analyzing psychological data; measure mental traits, abilities, and processes.
A pattern of abnormality evidenced by emotions, behaviors, or thoughts inappropriate to the situation that lead to personal distress or the inability to achieve important goals.
The use of psychotropic drugs to treat mental disorders.
Study of the relationship between physical energy and psychological experiences.
Reality distortion evidenced by highly disordered thought processes.
Any surgical technique in which neural pathways in the brain are cut in order to change behavior, including lobotomy.

Eysenck's personality dimension that measures our level of tough-mindedness, how hostile, ruthless, and insensitive we are; as opposed to tender-mindedness, how friendly, empathetic, and cooperative we are.
The early adolescent period marked by accelerated growth and onset of the ability to reproduce.
An aversive consequence that follows a voluntary behavior, thereby decreasing the probability the behavior will be repeated.
Small, adjustable opening in the iris of the eye that is smaller in bright light and larger in darkness.
Research method similar to a controlled experiment but in which random assignment to groups is not possible. It can provide strong evidence suggesting cause and effect relationships.
Division of the sample into groups such that every individual has an equal chance of being put in any group or condition.
Choosing of members of a population such that every individual has an equal chance of being chosen.
The difference between the largest score and the smallest score (quick and dirty).
Cognitive treatment developed by Ellis which is based on confronting irrational thoughts; change in irrational thinking will lead to a change in irrational behavior.
Freudian defense mechanism that provides socially acceptable reasons for our inappropriate behavior.
Freudian defense mechanism involving acting in a manner exactly opposite to our true feelings.
According to Rogers, the positive and original organism we are before society imposes conditions of worth on us.
The manner in which the ego delays gratification and otherwise deals with the environment in a planned rational fashion (in Freudian theory).
Retrieval of previously learned information.
The gene that is hidden or not expressed when the genes for a trait are different.
The tendency to remember recent information; in the memorization of a list of words, the recency effect is evidenced by better recall of the words later in the list.
The characteristics of the person, the person's behavior, and the environment all affect one another in two-way causal relationships (according to Bandura).
Compliance technique used by groups; individuals feel obligated to go along with a request for a small donation if they have first accepted a small gift.
Identification of learned items when they are presented.
Retrieval of memories often distorted by adding, dropping, or changing details to fit a schema.
The simplest form of behavior.
The path over which the reflex travels that typically includes a receptor, sensory or afferent neuron, interneuron, motor or efferent neuron, and effector.
Freudian defense mechanism characterized by immature, pleasurable behavior of an earlier level of development.
The conscious repetition of information to either maintain information in STM or to encode it for storage into long-term memory.
Construct treated as a concrete, tangible object.
In operant conditioning, any event that strengthens the behavior it follows.
A measure of retention of memory that assesses the time saved compared to learning the first time when learning information again.
Consistency or repeatability of results.

Sleep stage when eyes dart about. About 80 percent dreaming, 5 to 6 times each night (about 20 percent of sleep time). Called paradoxical sleep because EEGs are similar to stage 1 and wakefulness, but we are in deep sleep with skeletal muscles paralyzed.
A treatment for depression involving repeated pulses through a magnetic coil positioned above the right eyebrow of the patient that does not result in memory loss.
Repetition of the methods used in a previous experiment to see whether the same methods will yield the same results.
Tendency to judge the likelihood of things according to how they relate to a prototype; in social psychology the pre-judgment of people in the same way.
Most frequently used Freudian defense mechanism, characterized by unconscious forgetting; pushing threatening thoughts, feelings, and memories into the unconscious mind.
Blocking of anxiety-provoking feelings and experiences in the process of psychoanalysis.
Second stage of Selye's general adaptation syndrome characterized by the use of “fight or flight” mechanisms to control, cope with, or flee from the stressful situation.
Mixed reactions of infants to their mothers in the Strange Situation. They may approach their mothers upon their return but, at the same time, continue to cry or even push their mothers away.
A network of neurons extending from the brainstem/hindbrain into the midbrain; essential to the regulation of sleep, wakefulness, arousal, and attention.
Light-sensitive surface in the back of the eye containing rods and cones that transduce light energy. Has layers of bipolar cells and ganglion cells that transmit visual information to the brain.
The process of getting information out of memory storage.
A stimulus that provides a trigger to get an item out of stored memory.
Recently learned information disrupts our ability to remember older information.
Involves memory loss for a segment of the past, usually around the time of an accident, such as a blow to the head.
Characteristic of Piaget's concrete operational stage, the logical negation of an operation, for example, if 4 + 2 = 6 then 6 - 2 = 4.

Photoreceptors that detect black, white, and gray and movement; are necessary for peripheral and dim-light vision when cones do not respond. Distributed throughout the retina of the eye, except in the fovea.
Ascribed social positions in groups and defined behavior expectations.
The newborn's tendency to move its head when stroked on the cheek, turn toward the stimulus as if searching for a nipple, and open its mouth.
A projective test in which a person is shown a series of symmetrical inkblots and asked to describe what he or she thinks they represent.
Rapid conduction of impulses when the axon is myelinated since depolarizations jump from node (of Ranvier) to node.
The subgroup of the population that participates in the study.
Absence of hunger.
Individuals otherwise considered mentally retarded who have a specific exceptional skill typically in calculating, music, or art.
Attributes prejudice to frustration; when own self-worth is in doubt or jeopardy, we find others to blame.
An emotion is inferred from physiological arousal, and label of that emotion is based on our cognitive explanation for the arousal.
Framework of basic ideas and preconceptions about people, objects, and events based on past experience in long-term memory; concepts or frameworks that organize and interpret information.
A serious schizophrenic spectrum disorder characterized by thought disturbances, hallucinations, anxiety, emotional withdrawal, and delusions.
A schema for an event.

A mood disorder characterized by depression, lethargy, sleep disturbances, and craving for carbohydrates; generally occurs during the winter, when the amount of daylight is low, and is sometimes treated with exposure to bright lights.
Learning procedure in which a well-learned conditioned stimulus is paired with a new neutral stimulus resulting in a similar conditioned response.
Internal mechanism directing learned behavior as being desired, such as power and wealth.
Something seen as rewarding because it is associated with a primary reinforcer.
A characteristic apparent in only certain situations. Our unique pattern of traits determines our behavior.
The nonreproductive sexual characteristics including developed breasts in females; facial hair, Adam's apple, and deepened voice in males; and pubic hair and underarm hair in both.
After absence baby is happy to see mother, receptive to her contact. Securely attached babies tend to become socially competent children.
Focusing of awareness on a specific stimulus (while excluding others) in sensory memory.
The realization of our true intellectual and emotional potential (according to Maslow).
According to Jung, our sense of wholeness or unity.
Consciousness of oneself as a person.
Our overall view of our abilities, behavior, and personality or what we know about ourselves.
How competent and able we feel to accomplish tasks; an expectation of success.
How worthy we think we are.
A tendency to let our preconceived expectations of others influence how we treat them and thus evoke those very expectations.
Determining how new information relates to us personally.
Most common personality assessment technique, involves person answering a series of questions such as a personality questionnaire or supplying information about himself or herself.
Our tendency to take personal credit for our achievements and blame failures on situational factors; to perceive ourselves favorably.
Information processed for meaning into short-term memory and long-term memory.
A type of long-term memory that includes general knowledge, objective facts, and vocabulary.
Model of long-term memory with more irregular and distorted systems than strict hierarchies, with multiple links from one concept to others.
A set of rules we use to derive meaning from morphemes, words, and sentences.
The process by which we detect physical energy from our environment and encode it as neural signals.
Piaget's first stage (0-2 years) during which the infant experiences the world through senses and action patterns; progresses from reflexes to object permanence and symbolic thinking.
A temporary decrease in sensitivity to a stimulus that occurs when stimulation is unchanging.
Primitive, brief type of memory that holds incoming information just long enough for further processing.
Cell typically in sense organs that initiates action potentials which then travel along sensory/afferent neurons to the CNS.
A set of fearful responses, such as crying, arousal, and clinging to the caregiver, that infants exhibit when the caregiver attempts to leave the infant.
The tendency to remember and recall information that comes at the beginning (primacy effect) and at the end of a list of words (recency effect) more easily than those in the middle.
A neurotransmitter associated with arousal, sleep, appetite, moods, and emotions. A lack of serotonin is associated with depression.
A preset natural body weight, determined by the number of fat cells in our body.
Recessive genes located on the X chromosome with no corresponding gene on the Y chromosome result in expression of recessive trait more frequently in males.
The direction of an individual's sexual interest.
Masters and Johnson's four stages of bodily response during sex: excitement, plateau, orgasm, and resolution.
According to Jung represents our baser instinctual urges we attempt to keep hidden from others.
Encoding into memory superficial sensory information without making it relevant that seldom results in enduring memory.
Positively reinforcing closer and closer approximations of a desired behavior through operant conditioning.
Also called working memory, which can hold about seven unrelated items for about 20 to 30 seconds without rehearsal.
In classical conditioning the CS and UCS are paired together at the same time; weaker conditioning technique than the ideal delayed conditioning.
Maintains that minimum threshold varies with fatigue, attention, expectations, motivation, and emotional distress, as well as from one person to another.
Stressful changes in our lives such as death of a loved one, marriage, starting college, etc.
Research design in which participants don't know whether they are in the experimental or control group.
Inferences that a person's behavior is caused by some temporary condition or situation the person is in.
A complex combination of states of consciousness each with its own level of consciousness, awareness, responsiveness, and physiological arousal.
Temporary cessations of breathing that awaken the sufferer repeatedly during the night.
Most frequently a childhood sleep disruption that occurs during NREM-3 sleep characterized by trips out of bed or carrying on of complex activities.
Idea that society has certain age expectations for when someone should marry and have kids and people feel compelled to meet these expectations or face a crisis.
Refers to the way people gather, use, and interpret information about the social aspects of the world around them.
Involve being torn in different directions by opposing motives that block us from attaining a goal, leaving us feeling frustrated and stressed.
Improved performance of well- learned tasks in front of others.
Two or more people sharing common goals and interests interact and influence behavior of the other(s).
Worsened performance of a newly learned or difficult task when performed in front of an audience.
Babies are biologically equipped for learning language, which may be activated or constrained by experience.
Bandura's idea that we can learn behavior from others by first observing it and then imitating it.
The tendency of individuals to put less effort into group projects than when they are individually accountable.
Learned needs that energize behavior; acquired as part of growing up in a particular society or culture.
Psychologists who focus on how a person's mental life and behavior are shaped by interactions with other people.
The study of how groups influence the attitudes and behavior of the individual.
Observing the behavior of others in social situations to obtain information or guidance.
Cognitive behavioral therapy where the therapist can model the behavior for the client and then place the client in a simulated situation for practice.
Study of the biological basis of social behavior.
Psychological perspective concerned with how cultural differences affect behavior.
Subdivision of PNS that includes motor nerves that stimulate skeletal (voluntary) muscle.

Characterized by physical symptoms including pain and high anxiety in these individuals about having a disease. Patients need to have complained about, taken medicine for, changed lifestyle because of, or seen a physician about the symptoms and experienced anxiety that has interfered with carrying on normal activities for 6 months.
The skin sensations: touch/pressure, warmth, cold, and pain.
William Sheldon's theory that body types determine personality.
The process by which you determine the location of a sound.
Cattell's underlying 16 traits that guide your behavior.
Measures how fast you can answer questions in a specified time period.
Portion of the central nervous system below the medulla oblongata.
A method where the score on one half of the test questions is compared with the score on the other half of the questions to see if they are consistent.
The reappearance of a previously extinguished CR after a rest period.
Deals with the issue of whether or not personality traits present during infancy persist throughout the lifespan.
A measure of the average difference between each score and the mean of the data set; the square root of the variance.

Two-part test development procedure that first establishes test norms by giving the test to a large representative sample of those for whom the test is designed, and then ensures that the test is both administered and scored uniformly for all test takers.
Set of tasks administered under standard conditions to assess an individual's knowledge, skill, or personality characteristics.
Terman's revision of Binet's original individual IQ test.
When exposed to a loud noise or sudden drop, the neonate automatically arches his or her back, flings his or her limbs out, and quickly retracts them..
Tendency to recall information better if you are in the same internal state as when the information was encoded.

Condition that exists when the probability that the observed findings are due to chance is less than 1 in 20 (p < .05) according to some psychologists or less than 1 in 100 (p < .01) according to those with more stringent standards.
Field that involves the analysis of numerical data about representative samples of populations..
Overgeneralized belief about the characteristics of members of a particular group; schema used to quickly judge others.
Anxiety that influences members of a group concerned that their performance will confirm a negative stereotype.

Psychoactive drugs that activate motivational centers and reduce activity in inhibitory centers of the central nervous system by increasing activity of serotonin, dopamine, and norepinephrine neurotransmitter systems; include caffeine, nicotine, amphetamines, and cocaine.
A change in the environment that can be detected by sensory receptors; elicits (brings about) a response.
The retention of encoded information over time.
The fear of strangers that infants develop at around 8 months of age.
The process by which we appraise and respond to environmental threats.
Stimuli such as heat, cold, pain, that are perceived as endangering our well-being.
According to Adler, this tendency is a result of a need to compensate for our feelings of inferiority.
Early psychological perspective that emphasized units of consciousness and identification of elements of thought using introspection.
Freudian defense mechanism, expression of sexual or aggressive impulses redirected into more socially acceptable behaviors.
Receiving messages below your absolute threshold for conscious awareness.
The automatic response of drawing in anything at the mouth.
Folding-in portions of convolutions of the cerebral cortex.
The third part of Freud's personality systems which makes us feel proud when we obey its strict morality and feel guilt when we give in to the id's more pleasure-seeking urges.
Idiosyncratic, unimportant behavior associated with anticipation of a reward as a result of unintended reinforcement.
Cattell's cluster of personality traits which stems from deep source traits; the person we see on the outside.
Research method that obtains large samples of abilities, beliefs, or behaviors at a specific time and place through questionnaire or interview.
Automatic contraction of throat muscles that enables food to pass into the esophagus without our choking.
Subdivision of PNS and ANS whose stimulation results in responses that help the body deal with stressful events.
The replacement of one behavior that has been eliminated with another.

Region of communication between the transmitting presynaptic neuron and receiving postsynaptic neuron or muscle or gland, consisting of the presynaptic terminal buttons, a tiny space, and receptor sites typically on the postsynaptic dendrites.
Rules that are used to order words into grammatically sensible sentences.

A condition in which one sense (e.g., taste) is simultaneously perceived as if by one or more additional senses such as sight. Another form of synesthesia joins objects such as letters, shapes, numbers or people's names with a sensory perception such as smell, color, or flavor.
Behavior treatment for phobias in which the client is trained to relax to increasingly fearful stimuli.
Serious side effects from antipsychotic drugs including problems walking, drooling, and involuntary muscle spasms.
Negative response to particular foods that may be inborn and/or acquired through classical conditioning.
Recessive trait that produces progressive loss of nervous function and death in a baby.
Meaningful two-word sentences, usually a noun and a verb, and usually in the correct order uttered by 2-year-olds.
An infant's natural disposition to show a particular mood at a particular intensity for a specific period.
In classical conditioning, the presentation of the UCS at specific periods; time serves as the CS.
Side regions of cerebral cortex that are primary areas for hearing, understanding language (Wernicke's area), understanding music/ tonality, and processing smell.
Harmful substance (drug or virus) with which contact during the prenatal period can cause birth defect(s).
Tips at the end of axons which secrete neurotransmitters when stimulated by the action potential.
Gonads in males that produce hormones necessary for reproduction and development of secondary sex characteristics.
Part of forebrain that relays visual, auditory, taste, somatosensory (skin sensation) information to and from appropriate areas of cerebral cortex; involved in encoding sensory memory into STM.
Study of death and dying; Kübler-Ross's five stages of facing death: denial, anger, bargaining, depression, and acceptance.
A projective test composed of ambiguous pictures about which a person is asked to write a complete story.
Organized sets of concepts that explain phenomena.
Involves mental images, symbols, concepts, and rules of language.
Endocrine gland in neck that produces thyroxin, which stimulates and maintains metabolic activities.
The quality of a sound determined by the purity of a waveform; a note of the same pitch and loudness sounds different on different musical instruments.
Retrieval problem that involves known information that can only be retrieved incompletely; better cues are required for retrieval.
A program used in institutions in which a person's acceptable behavior is reinforced with tokens that can be exchanged for special privileges or goods.
Condition in which diminished effectiveness of drug necessitates larger dosages to produce desired effect.
Information processing guided by preexisting knowledge or expectations to construct perceptions; concept-driven.
In classical conditioning, the CS is presented first, removed, and then the UCS is presented.
A relatively permanent and stable characteristic that can be used to predict behavior.
Transformation of stimulus energy to the electrochemical energy of neural impulses.
In psychoanalysis, the venting of emotions both positive and negative by patients; treating their analyst as the symbolic representative of someone important in their past.
Bandura's scheme that our personal traits, the environment, and our behavior all interact to account for our behavior.
Trying possible solutions and discarding those that fail to solve the problem.
Robert Sternberg's idea of three separate and testable intelligences: analytical (facts), practical (“street smarts”), creative (seeing multiple solutions).

Proposed mechanism for color vision with cones that are differentially sensitive to different wavelengths of light; each color seen results from a specific ratio of activation among the three types of receptors.
A group of symptoms in females with only one X sex chromosome, including shortness, sterility, webbed neck, and difficulty with calculations.
Hard-driving, competitive, impatient, and ambitious individuals.
More relaxed and calm individuals.
Rogers's term for acceptance, value, and love from others independent of how we behave.
In classical conditioning, the unlearned, naturally occurring response (reaction) to the unconditioned stimulus.
In classical conditioning, the stimulus (change) that naturally and automatically triggers the reflexive unconditioned response (UR).

The level of consciousness of which we are unaware, which may include unacceptable feelings, wishes, and thoughts not directly available to conscious awareness, according to psychodynamic psychologists/psychoanalysts. According to cognitive psychologists, the unconscious is the level of consciousness that parallel processes information of which we are unaware.
Characterized by loss of responsiveness to the environment resulting from disease, trauma, or anesthesia.
Simple schizophrenia characterized by fragments of the symptoms of other, different types of schizophrenia.
Characterized by few demands, low responsiveness, little communication, and general detachment from a child's life.
The extent to which an instrument measures or predicts what it is supposed to.
The spread or dispersion of a set of research data or distribution.
Schedule of reinforcement in which responses are reinforced after varying lengths of time (in operant conditioning).
Schedule of reinforcement in which reinforcement is presented after a varying number of responses (in operant conditioning).

Originally called the satiety center, or “off” button, for hunger. When stimulated, it turns off the urge to eat and when removed, the organism will continue to eat excessively and gain weight rapidly.
Body sense of equilibrium with hairlike receptors in semicircular canals and vestibular sac in the inner ear.
Dominance of vision when there is a conflict among senses.
The encoding of pictorial images into our memory.
Difference thresholds increase in proportion to the size of the stimulus.
The most widely used measurement of intelligence; three age-related individual IQ tests (WPPSI, WISC, WAIS) that provide two scores, verbal and performance.
Region in left temporal lobe that plays role in understanding language and making meaningful sentences.
Intense craving for a drug accompanied by effects opposite of those the drug usually induces.
Range of scores for variables being measured for a group of individuals.
Horney's counterpart to penis envy of Freudian theory; male's desire to procreate.
For easy tasks, moderately high arousal is needed to do well; for difficult tasks, moderately low; and most average tasks, moderate level of arousal.

According to Vygotsky, the range between the level at which a child can solve a problem working alone with difficulty and the level at which a child can solve a problem with the assistance of adults or more-skilled children.
A fertilized egg with the genetic instructions for a new individual normally contained in 46 chromosomes.
